input:
In this worked example, we will estimate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor that is used to compress air. The compressor raises the air from a pressure of 1 bar up to a pressure of 6 bar, and the air enters the machine at an inlet temperature of 303 K. In order to carry out the estimate, the compression is treated as isentropic, which is an idealised process in which the compression is both reversible and adiabatic, and the heat-capacity ratio of air is taken as 1.4.

Under the isentropic assumption, the temperature of the gas rises as its pressure is increased, with the discharge temperature being determined by the inlet temperature together with the pressure ratio across the machine and the heat-capacity ratio of the gas. Carrying out the calculation with the values given above, the discharge temperature of the compressor is found to be 506 K.

It is important to appreciate, however, that this figure is obtained from an idealised estimate from which mechanical losses have been deliberately excluded. Real machines inevitably experience such losses, and as a consequence the discharge temperature that is actually measured on the installed machine is higher than the value estimated here. The isentropic figure should therefore be understood as an ideal benchmark against which the performance of the real machine can be compared, rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will be observed in practice.
target:
Calculate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor raising air from 1 bar to 6 bar, with an inlet temperature of 303 K. The compression is taken as isentropic and the heat-capacity ratio of air as 1.4.

Isentropic compression is reversible and adiabatic: no heat crosses the boundary and no loss is charged inside the machine. Those are the assumptions, and they stand before the result because the result depends on them. For an isentropic compression the discharge temperature is set by the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio, and the heat-capacity ratio; substitution of the stated values gives a discharge temperature of 506 K.

Along the compression the pressure and the temperature rise together, and the heat-capacity ratio controls the rise: at a fixed pressure ratio, a gas with the larger ratio returns the larger temperature rise. The inlet temperature sets the level the rise starts from, so the same machine discharges hotter on a hotter inlet at unchanged pressures.

The check on the estimate is the installed machine. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, and the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher. The direction of the difference is the one the assumptions predict: losses the model omits appear in the real machine as additional temperature rise. The estimate is therefore the lower bound of the pair, and it is used as such: a measured temperature close to it speaks for the machine's condition, and a measured temperature well above it is the deviation that needs explaining, not the estimate.
